title: What a penetration test actually tells you
excerpt: A penetration test is not a pass mark. It is a record of what an attacker could do on a particular day, and what you should fix first.
author: Shakir

blocks.text: A penetration test is often bought for the wrong reason. Someone needs a certificate for procurement, a customer has asked for evidence, or a board wants reassurance before a launch. Those are legitimate reasons to commission a test, but none of them describe what a test actually produces.

What you get is a sample. A good tester, working within an agreed scope, for a fixed number of days, will find some of the ways an attacker could reach something that matters. The absence of a finding does not mean the absence of a weakness. It means this particular tester did not find it in the time available.

The most useful conversation happens before testing starts. Which systems are in scope? Which accounts and environments? Is this a production test or a staging test? What is out of bounds, and why? A test that avoids production because of risk is not necessarily a bad test, but the report should say so plainly.

A narrow scope is not a problem if it reflects the real risk. A wide scope with no priorities usually produces a long report and a short list of decisions. We would rather test the three paths that lead to patient records than spend two weeks enumerating login pages.
The report is not the deliverable

A report that lists findings without owners, dates, and remediation guidance is trivia. The deliverable is a smaller attack surface. That means someone has to decide what to fix, someone has to fix it, and someone has to check that the fix holds. A retest is not an upsell; it is the part that closes the loop.

items: A clear scope, test window, and list of exclusions
Reproducible steps, not just a severity label
The business impact of each finding in plain language
A severity rationale that explains the rating
Remediation guidance specific to your stack
A retest of the items marked as fixed

blocks.text: What to ask before you buy

items: Who will do the work, and what have they tested before?
How will the test be scoped, and who signs off on the scope?
Will the test touch production, and how will you protect live data?
Is remediation support included, or does the relationship end with the PDF?
Is a retest included, and what counts as fixed?
How will findings be shared during the engagement if something critical appears?

blocks.text: The goal is not a clean report. The goal is a smaller attack surface.

Security is a moving target. A test is a snapshot of one configuration, one release, and one set of assumptions. The organisations that get value from testing treat it as part of a cycle: test, fix, retest, change something, test again. The organisations that get less value treat it as a certificate to file.

If you are commissioning your first test, start with the system that would hurt most if it were compromised. Make the scope small enough to do properly. Ask for a debrief, not just a document. Then put the fixes in the same backlog as the rest of the work, with dates and owners. That is the difference between buying a test and reducing risk.
